agree.reason: The open budget and the admission that this is a first game will reassure some readers, but someone who has lost money on a campaign that never shipped will notice there's no delivery date, no refund plan and only a vague 'reserve', so they probably won't pledge yet.

honest.reason: The draft doesn't claim the game is a 'proven hit', but it overstates elsewhere: the heading says 'hundreds of tables' when the brief gives 140 sessions, and it invents 'four winters of playtesting', 'every session changed something', a mix of tester types and a 'locked in' quote.

works_the_facts.reason: It derives no figures: it never shows that about 572 backers at $49 reach the goal, that 1,500 copies would cost $30,900 to make and ship (more than the goal), or what dollar amount 'the rest' leaves for fees and reserve, so the claim that the goal covers everything isn't shown.

right_comparison.reason: It never compares this campaign with what the reader could otherwise do, such as waiting for retail or backing an experienced creator, and it doesn't measure the 1,240 signups against the roughly 572 backers needed to fund.

qualification.reason: The risks section promises 'real dates' but gives none, and it names no delivery month, no size for the reserve and no consequence if something is missed, so a reader has nothing to check.

objections.reason: It deals with the first-time-creator worry head-on and shows where the money goes, but it skips the questions this reader would ask most: when the game ships, whether the margin covers fees, and what happens to backers' money if production fails.

fit.reason: It is roughly 500 words with suitable pitch sections, though it still contains bracketed placeholders and drops the 'proven hit' framing the brief asked for without saying so.
